question: True or false: SPF 50 sunscreen blocks almost twice as much sunburn-causing radiation as SPF 30.
source_excerpt: SPF 30 filters about 97% of UVB rays, and SPF 50 filters about 98%.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the SPF number scales protection linearly, so 50 should be close to twice as strong as 30. In fact both already block almost all burning rays, and the difference is about one percentage point.
extra.verification_notes: SPF 30 filters ~97% of UVB and SPF 50 ~98%, so SPF 50 does not block almost twice as much (https://www.wlrn.org/light/health/2026-05-29/do-you-need-spf-30-50-or-100-we-answer-your-burning-sunscreen-questions).

explanation: SPF 30 already stops about 97% of burning UVB rays, and SPF 50 stops about 98%, so the jump is only around one percentage point. How thickly you apply it and how often you reapply matter far more than the number.

question: Which large African animal spends its days half-submerged in rivers and oozes a reddish fluid from its skin that works as its own natural sunscreen?
source_excerpt: Hipposudoric acid is a red pigment found in the skin secretions of the hippopotamus.

extra.why_interesting: Most people think sunscreen is a purely human invention. One big African animal makes its own, and its red sweat is a famous myth with a real job behind it. Players can work it out from the clues: large, African, spends hours in the sun and water.
extra.verification_notes: Hippos secrete a red fluid (hipposudoric acid) that acts as sunscreen and antimicrobial, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hipposudoric_acid; no newer development contradicts this.

explanation: Hippos secrete a red-orange liquid, long mistaken for 'blood sweat', whose pigments absorb ultraviolet light and may even help fight germs. It is a built-in sunscreen for an animal with almost no hair.
